mcq.q: Which climate type shows the largest gap between summer and winter temperatures?
choices: A Maritime
B Mediterranean
C Continental
D Coastal fog belt
mcq.answer: C Continental
mcq.why: Continental climates are far from the sea, so summers are hot and winters cold.

mcq.q: In a high-rainfall vineyard, a cover crop between the rows is used mainly to
choices: A Raise the water table
B Compete with the vine for water and vigour
C Warm the soil in spring
D Replace the need for rootstocks
mcq.answer: B Compete with the vine for water and vigour
mcq.why: Cover crops take water and nutrients, lower vigour, and can improve soil structure.

mcq.q: Machine harvesting is generally unsuitable when the aim is to
choices: A Pick a large block of healthy fruit quickly at night
B Select only noble-rot or unevenly ripe bunches
C Supply a high-volume white press house
D Keep harvest labour costs down
mcq.answer: B Select only noble-rot or unevenly ripe bunches
mcq.why: Botrytis and selective picking need hand work; machines take everything.

mcq.q: Malolactic conversion typically
choices: A Raises malic acidity and adds banana notes
B Converts malic acid to lactic acid and can add a buttery note
C Stops alcoholic fermentation while sugar remains
D Strips colour from red must
mcq.answer: B Converts malic acid to lactic acid and can add a buttery note
mcq.why: MLF softens acidity (malic to lactic) and may produce diacetyl.

mcq.q: Compared with large old casks, new 225-litre barriques give a wine
choices: A Less oak flavour and less oxygen uptake
B More oak flavour and more oxygen uptake
C No oak flavour but more reduction
D Only toast aroma and no tannin
mcq.answer: B More oak flavour and more oxygen uptake
mcq.why: Small new oak has more wood-to-wine contact and lets in more oxygen.

mcq.q: The main reason sulphur dioxide is added at bottling is to
choices: A Deepen colour in red wines
B Start malolactic conversion
C Protect against oxidation and microbes
D Increase residual sugar
mcq.answer: C Protect against oxidation and microbes
mcq.why: SO2 is an antioxidant and antimicrobial.

mcq.q: A short cold soak before red fermentation is used mainly to extract
choices: A Harsh seed tannin at high temperature
B Colour and flavour at low temperature with limited tannin
C Alcohol without skins
D Lactic acid from malic acid
mcq.answer: B Colour and flavour at low temperature with limited tannin
mcq.why: Aqueous extraction in the cold pulls colour and aroma ahead of alcoholic tannin.

mcq.q: Everyday white wines are usually fermented cool in stainless steel in order to
choices: A Encourage wild-yeast complexity and oxidation
B Preserve primary fruit and limit oxidation
C Guarantee malolactic conversion
D Extract seed tannin
mcq.answer: B Preserve primary fruit and limit oxidation
mcq.why: Cool, protective ferments keep thiols and esters and avoid browning.

mcq.q: In the Médoc, the dominant grape in a typical classified-growth blend is
choices: A Merlot
B Cabernet Franc
C Cabernet Sauvignon
D Petit Verdot
mcq.answer: C Cabernet Sauvignon
mcq.why: Left Bank gravel suits Cabernet Sauvignon; Merlot is the usual partner.

mcq.q: Pomerol is distinctive among Bordeaux appellations because it
choices: A Is classified in the 1855 ranking
B Has no official classification and is Merlot-led
C Must be 100% Cabernet Sauvignon
D Produces only sweet white wine
mcq.answer: B Has no official classification and is Merlot-led
mcq.why: Pomerol was never classified; clay and Merlot define the style.

mcq.q: The principal grape of Sauternes, and the one most prone to noble rot, is
choices: A Sauvignon Blanc
B Muscadelle
C Sémillon
D Ugni Blanc
mcq.answer: C Sémillon
mcq.why: Thin-skinned Sémillon takes botrytis; Sauvignon Blanc adds acidity.

mcq.q: Village Chablis is typically fermented and aged in
choices: A New small barriques for coconut oak
B Stainless steel or old oak, to keep a lean citrus style
C Amphorae with extended skin contact
D Bottle under flor
mcq.answer: B Stainless steel or old oak, to keep a lean citrus style
mcq.why: Unoaked or neutrally oaked Chablis shows cool-climate acidity and limestone.

mcq.q: The Côte de Nuits is best known for
choices: A White Grand Cru Chardonnay
B Red Pinot Noir, including many of Burgundy’s red Grand Crus
C Sparkling Aligoté only
D Sweet Gamay
mcq.answer: B Red Pinot Noir, including many of Burgundy’s red Grand Crus
mcq.why: Most red Grand Crus sit on the Côte de Nuits; Beaune holds most of the whites.

mcq.q: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé are both made principally from
choices: A Chenin Blanc
B Sauvignon Blanc
C Melon de Bourgogne
D Pinot Gris
mcq.answer: B Sauvignon Blanc
mcq.why: Central Loire AOC whites from Sauvignon Blanc; Pouilly-Fumé can show a smoky note.

mcq.q: Savennières is a dry wine from
choices: A Sauvignon Blanc on flint in the Central Vineyards
B Chenin Blanc on schist in Anjou
C Melon de Bourgogne near Nantes
D Viognier on granite in the Northern Rhône
mcq.answer: B Chenin Blanc on schist in Anjou
mcq.why: Savennières is age-worthy dry Chenin from Anjou.

mcq.q: Condrieu must be made from
choices: A Marsanne
B Roussanne
C Viognier
D Clairette
mcq.answer: C Viognier
mcq.why: Condrieu (and Château-Grillet) are Viognier AOCs.

mcq.q: Châteauneuf-du-Pape reds are typically
choices: A Cool-climate 100% Syrah aged only in new barriques
B Warm-climate Grenache-based blends, often on galet stones
C Ice wines from late-picked Clairette
D White wines from Picpoul only
mcq.answer: B Warm-climate Grenache-based blends, often on galet stones
mcq.why: Southern Rhône heat and GSM blends; large old oak or concrete is common.

mcq.q: An Alsace Grand Cru still wine is usually labelled with
choices: A A blend name and no variety
B The vineyard name and, in most cases, a single variety
C Only the word Edelzwicker
D A Prädikat such as Spätlese
mcq.answer: B The vineyard name and, in most cases, a single variety
mcq.why: Alsace Grand Cru is typically a named site and a noble variety.

mcq.q: Barolo is made from Nebbiolo grown in
choices: A Veneto
B Tuscany
C Piedmont
D Alto Adige
mcq.answer: C Piedmont
mcq.why: Barolo and Barbaresco are the Langhe Nebbiolo DOCG wines.

mcq.q: Brunello di Montalcino must be
choices: A A Sangiovese–Cabernet blend aged two years
B 100% Sangiovese with a long minimum ageing period
C Merlot from the Chianti hills
D White Trebbiano from coastal Tuscany
mcq.answer: B 100% Sangiovese with a long minimum ageing period
mcq.why: Brunello is 100% Sangiovese (locally Brunello) and is released after lengthy ageing.

mcq.q: Amarone della Valpolicella is dry because
choices: A Fermentation is stopped with spirit
B Dried grapes are fermented to dryness after appassimento
C The wine is a sparkling tank wine
D It is a pale rosé from short maceration
mcq.answer: B Dried grapes are fermented to dryness after appassimento
mcq.why: Appassimento concentrates sugar; a full ferment yields a dry, high-alcohol red.

mcq.q: The principal grape of Soave is
choices: A Pinot Grigio
B Garganega
C Vermentino
D Cortese
mcq.answer: B Garganega
mcq.why: Soave is Garganega, sometimes with Trebbiano di Soave or Chardonnay.

mcq.q: For a red Rioja Gran Reserva, the legal minimum ageing is
choices: A One year in total, six months in oak
B Two years in total, one in oak
C Three years in total, one in oak
D Five years in total, two in oak
mcq.answer: D Five years in total, two in oak
mcq.why: Gran Reserva red: 5 years before release, at least 2 of them in oak.

mcq.q: Priorat’s distinctive vineyard soil is
choices: A Chalk with fossil oyster shells
B Llicorella slate and mica
C Terra rossa over limestone
D Deep river silt
mcq.answer: B Llicorella slate and mica
mcq.why: Llicorella forces low yields and gives a mineral, concentrated style.

mcq.q: Rías Baixas is best known for dry wines from
choices: A Verdejo
B Albariño
C Godello only
D Tempranillo blanco
mcq.answer: B Albariño
mcq.why: Albariño from Galicia: high acid, peach and citrus, often lees-aged.

mcq.q: A German Prädikat (Kabinett through Trockenbeerenauslese) tells you
choices: A The residual sugar in the bottled wine
B The must weight of the grapes at harvest
C The exact vineyard classification
D That the wine is always trocken
mcq.answer: B The must weight of the grapes at harvest
mcq.why: Prädikat is ripeness at harvest; the wine may still be fermented dry.

mcq.q: Santorini’s leading white grape, grown on volcanic soils, is
choices: A Moschofilero
B Assyrtiko
C Agiorgitiko
D Xinomavro
mcq.answer: B Assyrtiko
mcq.why: Assyrtiko keeps acidity in a warm, windy, volcanic setting.

mcq.q: A typical Vinho Verde white is
choices: A Full-bodied, oaked and low in acid
B Light, high in acid, modest in alcohol, sometimes with a slight spritz
C A fortified Muscat
D A late-harvest sweet red
mcq.answer: B Light, high in acid, modest in alcohol, sometimes with a slight spritz
mcq.why: Coastal Minho: Alvarinho, Loureiro and others in a light, crisp style.

mcq.q: Unfortified Douro reds are usually based on
choices: A Baga and Castelão only
B Touriga Nacional and other Port varieties
C Alvarinho and Loureiro
D Palomino and Pedro Ximénez
mcq.answer: B Touriga Nacional and other Port varieties
mcq.why: The same grapes as Port, fermented dry for table wine.

mcq.q: Marlborough’s reputation was built on
choices: A Sweet sparkling Shiraz
B Pungent Sauvignon Blanc
C High-alcohol Zinfandel
D Flor-aged Palomino
mcq.answer: B Pungent Sauvignon Blanc
mcq.why: Cool, sunny Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc defined modern New Zealand.

mcq.q: Mendoza Malbec benefits chiefly from
choices: A Sea-level humidity and frequent autumn rain
B High altitude, bright light and Andes meltwater
C Constant coastal fog like Casablanca
D Winter freeze for icewine
mcq.answer: B High altitude, bright light and Andes meltwater
mcq.why: Altitude cools the nights; irrigation comes from the Andes.

mcq.q: Coonawarra Cabernet Sauvignon is associated with
choices: A Terra rossa over limestone
B Schist terraces above a river
C Volcanic black sand
D Granite sand in a granite cirque
mcq.answer: A Terra rossa over limestone
mcq.why: The thin red soil over limestone is Coonawarra’s hallmark.

mcq.q: The Willamette Valley is most closely associated with
choices: A Hot-climate Cabernet Sauvignon
B Pinot Noir in a moderate, often cloudy climate
C Fortified Muscat
D Bush-vine Pinotage
mcq.answer: B Pinot Noir in a moderate, often cloudy climate
mcq.why: Oregon’s Willamette is a cool-to-moderate Pinot Noir region.

mcq.q: In the EU, a PDO wine compared with a PGI wine generally has
choices: A Fewer production rules and a larger area
B Stricter rules and a more tightly defined area
C No link to a geographic place
D A requirement to add spirit
mcq.answer: B Stricter rules and a more tightly defined area
mcq.why: PDO (AOP/DOCG and peers) is the tighter origin category.

mcq.q: If a US label names an AVA, at least this share of the grapes must come from that AVA
mcq.why: Federal AVA rule is 85% (some states set a higher bar).

mcq.q: Italian IGT sits in the quality pyramid
choices: A Above DOCG
B Between generic wine and DOC/DOCG, with more blending freedom
C Only for sparkling wine
D Only for sweet wine
mcq.answer: B Between generic wine and DOC/DOCG, with more blending freedom
mcq.why: IGT (PGI) is more flexible than DOC/DOCG and below them in the hierarchy.

mcq.q: The EU minimum time on lees for non-vintage Champagne is
choices: A 9 months
B 15 months
C 36 months
D 60 months
mcq.answer: B 15 months
mcq.why: NV Champagne: 15 months on lees; vintage: 36 months.

mcq.q: The Côte des Blancs in Champagne is planted mainly with
choices: A Pinot Noir
B Pinot Meunier
C Chardonnay
D Arbane
mcq.answer: C Chardonnay
mcq.why: Chalk slopes of the Côte des Blancs are the Chardonnay heartland.

mcq.q: Prosecco’s second fermentation is typically carried out
choices: A In bottle with riddling and disgorgement
B In tank (Charmat / Martinotti)
C In the grape berry before crush
D Under flor in a solera
mcq.answer: B In tank (Charmat / Martinotti)
mcq.why: Glera is fermented in tank to keep primary fruit; bottle method is rare.

mcq.q: Traditional Cava is based on
choices: A Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier only
B Macabeo, Xarel-lo and Parellada
C Glera and Verdiso
D Chenin Blanc and Cabernet Franc
mcq.answer: B Macabeo, Xarel-lo and Parellada
mcq.why: The three local varieties remain the core, though Chardonnay and Pinot are allowed.

mcq.q: A Champagne labelled Brut may contain residual sugar up to
choices: A 3 g/L
B 6 g/L
C 12 g/L
D 32 g/L
mcq.answer: C 12 g/L
mcq.why: Brut is 0–12 g/L; Extra Brut is 0–6; Extra Dry is 12–17.

mcq.q: Fino Sherry is aged
choices: A Oxidatively in a hot estufa
B Biologically under a flor yeast veil
C In bottle like Vintage Port
D On skins for three weeks
mcq.answer: B Biologically under a flor yeast veil
mcq.why: Flor protects Fino and Manzanilla and gives the yeasty, almond character.

mcq.q: Port is fortified
choices: A After the wine is fully dry
B During alcoholic fermentation so that residual sugar remains
C Before the grapes are crushed
D Only in the bottle after 20 years
mcq.answer: B During alcoholic fermentation so that residual sugar remains
mcq.why: Spirit is added mid-ferment; leftover sugar defines Port’s sweetness.

mcq.q: Vintage Port is typically aged
choices: A Ten years in wood, then drunk from the cask
B About two years in wood, then for many years in bottle
C Under flor in Sanlúcar
D In tank at low temperature like Ruby only
mcq.answer: B About two years in wood, then for many years in bottle
mcq.why: Short wood ageing, then slow bottle development; decant before service.

mcq.q: Pedro Ximénez Sherry is usually
choices: A A bone-dry biological wine
B Made from sun-dried PX grapes and is intensely sweet
C A pale tank sparkling wine
D A red VDN from Grenache
mcq.answer: B Made from sun-dried PX grapes and is intensely sweet
mcq.why: Sundried PX gives a black, raisiny, very sweet wine, often used to sweeten blends.

mcq.q: Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is
choices: A A dry Northern Rhône Viognier
B A vin doux naturel from Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains
C A tank-method sparkling dry wine
D An Australian Topaque
mcq.answer: B A vin doux naturel from Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains
mcq.why: Southern Rhône VDN: fortify a Muscat ferment to keep sweetness and aroma.

mcq.q: Cork taint (TCA) typically shows as
choices: A Vinegar and nail varnish
B Damp cardboard and a muted fruit character
C Rotten eggs that blow off with air
D Butter and cream from MLF
mcq.answer: B Damp cardboard and a muted fruit character
mcq.why: TCA suppresses fruit and adds a mouldy cardboard note; the wine is faulty.

mcq.q: A suitable service temperature for a light, dry white such as Muscadet is
choices: A 4–6 °C, ice-cold like a freezer
B Well chilled, about 7–10 °C
C Cellar-warm, 16–18 °C
D Room temperature above 20 °C
mcq.answer: B Well chilled, about 7–10 °C
mcq.why: Light whites and most sparkling wines are served well chilled, not frozen.

mcq.q: High-tannin red wines are most comfortable with dishes that are
choices: A Hot with fresh chilli and no fat
B High in protein and fat, such as grilled steak
C Very sweet desserts
D Delicate steamed white fish only
mcq.answer: B High in protein and fat, such as grilled steak
mcq.why: Protein and fat bind tannin; chilli and sweetness make tannin seem harsher.

mcq.q: Bottles closed with a natural cork are best stored
choices: A Upright in a sunny window
B On their side, cool, dark and with fairly steady temperature
C In a working freezer
D Next to a heat source to mature them faster
mcq.answer: B On their side, cool, dark and with fairly steady temperature
mcq.why: Side storage keeps the cork moist; heat, light and swings age wine badly.

parts.prompt: Outline the climate of the Bordeaux region and the vineyard factors that distinguish the Left Bank (Médoc and Graves) from the Right Bank (Saint-Émilion and Pomerol).
points: Maritime climate: Atlantic influence, Gulf Stream, moderate temperatures, rainfall through the year including at harvest.
Vintage variation is significant because of autumn rain and humidity.
Left Bank: free-draining gravel over clay/sand; gravel suits Cabernet Sauvignon (heat, drainage).
Médoc is cooler/wetter in the north; Graves slightly warmer; proximity to Gironde/Garonne moderates frost.
Right Bank: more clay, limestone and sand; clay suits Merlot (cooler, holds water).
Saint-Émilion limestone plateau and côtes vs Pomerol plateau with clay (and iron-rich crasse de fer in places).
Aspect and drainage on the côtes vs flatter Médoc; planting density often high on the Left Bank.
Award marks for any other accurate contrast (frost risk, harvest dates, blending need).

parts.prompt: Name the principal black grape varieties and explain how blending shapes style on each bank.
points: Cabernet Sauvignon: high tannin and acidity, blackcurrant, needs warm sites; core of Médoc blends.
Merlot: earlier ripening, softer tannin, plum/red fruit; dominant on the Right Bank and used to flesh out Left Bank wines.
Cabernet Franc: perfume, red fruit, used on both banks (more in Saint-Émilion).
Petit Verdot (and a little Malbec/Carménère historically): colour, spice, used in small amounts.
Blending manages vintage risk and builds complexity, colour, tannin and mid-palate.
Name a typical Left Bank vs Right Bank balance (e.g. Cabernet-led vs Merlot-led).

parts.prompt: Describe the winemaking choices that produce a full-bodied, age-worthy red Bordeaux.
points: Ripe harvest; sorting (especially in wet years).
Destemming; crush; fermentation on skins in wood, stainless or concrete.
Maceration long enough for colour and ripe tannin; punching down / pumping over.
Malolactic conversion, usually in tank or barrel.
Maturation in oak (often a high share of new French barriques for crus classés) for 12–24 months.
Racking, fining (egg white traditionally), blending after élevage.
Bottle age for structure to soften; high-volume wines use less new oak and shorter élevage.

parts.prompt: Name two specific appellations, one from each bank, and state a quality or style point for each.
points: Any accurate pair: e.g. Pauillac / Saint-Julien / Margaux / Pessac-Léognan vs Saint-Émilion Grand Cru / Pomerol.
Style point: Pauillac often firm, cedar and blackcurrant; Pomerol richer, plush Merlot.
Mention of 1855 or Saint-Émilion classification vs no Pomerol classification can score.
Do not invent AOCs.

parts.prompt: Compare the climate, soils and resulting style of Chablis with those of the Côte de Beaune.
points: Chablis: cool continental; frost risk in spring; short season; limestone/Kimmeridgian (and Portlandian on some sites).
Style: pale, high acid, green apple, lemon, wet stone; little or no new oak at village level.
Côte de Beaune: moderate continental, slightly warmer and more sheltered; limestone and marl on the Côte d’Or slope.
Style: more body and ripe citrus/stone fruit; village and Premier/Grand Cru often see oak.
Grand Cru Chablis can take old or some new oak but remains leaner than Beaune.
Premier Cru and Grand Cru in both places come from better aspect/drainage.
Mâconnais is warmer still (if mentioned as contrast, can score as extra).
Award for named villages: Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet, Chassagne-Montrachet vs Chablis Premiers such as Montée de Tonnerre.

parts.prompt: Explain how vineyard work and harvest decisions affect quality in these cool-climate Chardonnay regions.
points: Site: mid-slope, south/south-east aspect for ripeness and frost drainage.
Frost protection in Chablis: heaters, wind machines, aspersion.
Yield control: pruning, disbudding, green harvest; high yield dilutes and delays ripeness.
Canopy: enough leaf for sugar, enough air to limit rot in a wet year.
Disease pressure: downy/powdery mildew, grey rot in wet harvests.
Hand harvest for Premier/Grand Cru; sorting.
Harvest date: acid/sugar/flavour ripeness; too early is green, too late is flabby and rot-prone.
Old vines / low vigour soils linked to concentration.

parts.prompt: Outline typical winery choices for a village Meursault and for a village Chablis.
points: Both: whole-bunch or destemmed press, settle, alcoholic ferment with cultured or ambient yeast.
Chablis village: stainless or old wood, cool to mid temperature, often block MLF or only partial, short élevage on fine lees, little new oak.
Meursault village: barrel ferment common, a proportion of new oak, MLF usual, lees stirring for texture, 10–18 months in wood.
Both may be fined/filtered; quality wines avoid heavy manipulation.
State the style contrast: lean/mineral vs nutty/buttery/textured.
Mention of bâtonnage, reduction management, and SO2 use can score.

parts.prompt: Describe the climate and the main grape varieties of Champagne, and link each variety to a typical sub-region and the character it contributes to a blend.
points: Cool continental climate at the northern limit for ripening; frost, rain and vintage variation.
Chalk and limestone with a thin topsoil; good drainage and water reserve.
Pinot Noir: body, red fruit, structure — Montagne de Reims, Côte des Bar.
Pinot Meunier: fruit, early ripeness, useful in cooler/frost-prone sites — Vallée de la Marne.
Chardonnay: acidity, citrus, longevity, finesse — Côte des Blancs.
Most wines are blends of variety, village and vintage (reserve wines for NV).
Blanc de Blancs / Blanc de Noirs as named styles.
Award for other accurate vineyard points (pruning, yield, press fractions).

parts.prompt: Outline the traditional method as used in Champagne, from press to disgorgement.
points: Whole-bunch press; free-run (cuvée) separated from taille; settle.
Alcoholic ferment to a dry still base (vin clair), usually in tank, sometimes in oak.
Optional MLF; blending (assemblage) including reserve wines for NV.
Tirage: yeast + sugar; bottle; crown cap; second ferment creates CO2 and lees.
Lees ageing: autolysis (biscuit, brioche); NV ≥15 months, vintage ≥36 months.
Riddling (remuage) to bring sediment to the neck; disgorgement.
Dosage (liqueur d’expédition) sets sweetness; cork and muselet.
Further bottle rest before release.

parts.prompt: Contrast non-vintage Brut with a vintage Blanc de Blancs in style and typical use at the table.
points: NV Brut: house style, blended, usually lighter autolysis, widely used as an aperitif.
Vintage BdB: one year, Chardonnay only, longer lees, leaner, more age-worthy, citrus to toast.
Service: well chilled; flute or white-wine glass; vintage can take richer fish or poultry.
Dosage usually Brut for both; prestige or late-disgorged wines may be more complex.
Award for accurate food matches (oysters/aperitif vs creamy fish).

parts.prompt: Explain biological and oxidative ageing in Jerez and name the dry styles that result.
points: Palomino base wine, fortified: about 15% abv for biological, about 17%+ for oxidative (flor cannot survive).
Flor (yeast veil) consumes glycerol and alcohol, adds acetaldehyde (almond, dough), protects from oxygen: Fino and Manzanilla.
Manzanilla must be aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda (cooler, more persistent flor).
Oloroso: no flor, oxidative, nutty, fuller body, dry unless later sweetened.
Amontillado: begins under flor, then oxidative when flor dies or is lost.
Palo Cortado: rare, oxidative character with some amontillado-like aroma.
Solera and criadera system blends ages and keeps flor fed (for biological wines).
En rama as an unfiltered, more intense bottling can score.

parts.prompt: How is a sweet PX or Cream Sherry produced, and what is the typical residual-sugar contrast with Fino?
points: PX: Pedro Ximénez grapes sun-dried, fermented little, fortified, aged oxidatively; very high sugar.
Moscatel similar from Moscatel grapes.
Cream: usually sweetened Oloroso (PX added); Pale Cream is sweetened Fino-style.
Fino is dry (effectively no residual sugar); PX is lusciously sweet.
Mention of blending for commercial sweetness levels can score.

parts.prompt: Give storage and service advice for Fino or Manzanilla, and suggest one savoury food pairing with a reason.
points: Buy from a recent bottling; these wines are fragile once bottled.
Store upright, cool and dark; drink within months of bottling, days of opening (fridge).
Serve well chilled in a white-wine glass (not a tiny copita only).
Do not cellar Fino for bottle age the way you might an Oloroso or vintage Port.
Pairing: salted almonds, olives, jamón, fried fish — salt and fat stand up to acetaldehyde and dry finish.
Acidity and dryness cleanse oil; avoid very sweet dishes.
Award for contrasting service of Oloroso (less cold, nutty dishes or consommé).
